The delay in disclosure cost us three weeks.
The decision to publish the numbers was mine.
The acceptance of scrutiny is what made us credible.
The renewal of the contract required no negotiation.
The loss of their trust was the price of that delay.
The introduction of a weekly cadence changed the account.
I read your one-pager on the plane. It is the shortest thing you have ever sent me, and somehow it says more. Who cut it down?
I did. The first draft was two pages of verbs. The decision to publish, the delay in disclosure, the loss of their trust — once those became nouns, the page fit.
The board will stop at one line. You call the weekly report a permanent safeguard. Are you sure you want to promise that?
Yes. The introduction of that cadence is the only reason the account survived. Making it permanent is not a promise, it is a precedent.
And the oversight? If it sits with you, the board reads the whole thing as one person's habit.
It moves to operations in January. My name is on the mandate, not on the checklist.
One more thing. The candor paragraph is the best writing in the letter and it is also the riskiest. Investors read "our own bad numbers" and hear "more bad numbers are coming".
Then they will read the next sentence. The publication of those numbers is what made the good ones believable, and the rigor of the report is what keeps them honest.
The delay in disclosure cost us three weeks and two accounts.
The introduction of a weekly cadence is what saved the account.
The report is no longer a recovery measure but a permanent safeguard.
That is the mandate I am asking you to renew.

Izabel, it is Sofia. The board pack closes on Friday at noon, so this is the last window for changes to your letter. Three things you asked me to confirm before you send it. First, the numbers. The delay in disclosure was three weeks, not two; I went back to the warehouse log and the first warning is dated the eighth. Second, the cadence. The weekly report has now run for thirty-one consecutive Thursdays without a single miss, which is the line I would put in bold, because it is the one thing nobody can argue with. Third, the oversight. Legal is comfortable with the wording as long as you say the report moves to operations in January, and not that it has already moved, because it has not. One personal note, if you will allow it. I have read the whole letter twice and the paragraph on candor is the best thing in it. Do not let anyone shorten that one to make room for the charts.

Izabel, David Chen. Something happened this week that I thought you should hear from me rather than from your sales team. Our board asked purchasing for an example of a supplier report worth copying, and I gave them yours. Not the case study, the one-page summary. What convinced them was not the recovery; it was that the failure and the fix sit on the same page, in the same size of type. My chairman called it the first supplier document he had read in five years that did not need a translator. So expect a call from our procurement group, and expect them to ask for the template. My advice, and you may ignore it: do not give them a template. Give them the rule behind it. A template can be filled in badly by anyone, and the rigor is not in the format, it is in the habit of publishing the number before somebody asks you for it.
